lines.say: The typical US stock lost money. Minus six point nine percent.

lines.text: Yet from 1926 to 2025, the whole market turned $1 into $15,401.
lines.say: Yet from 1926 to 2025, the whole market turned one dollar into fifteen thousand four hundred one dollars.

lines.text: How? Of $91 trillion in wealth created, half came from just 46 companies.
lines.say: How? Of ninety-one trillion dollars in wealth created, half came from just forty-six companies.

scene.label: Firms behind half of $91T in wealth, 1926-2025

lines.text: Squirrel can't tell which little tree becomes the giant. So squirrel hides acorns under lots of trees.
lines.say: Squirrel can't tell which little tree becomes the giant. So squirrel hides acorns under lots of trees.

lines.text: One-tree version: at the end of 2000, 62% of Enron's 401(k) plan was Enron stock.
lines.say: The one-tree version? At the end of the year two thousand, sixty-two percent of Enron's four-oh-one-k plan was Enron stock.

scene.label: Enron 401(k) assets in Enron stock, end of 2000

lines.text: Then Enron shares fell from $90.75 to 26 cents in about 15 months.
lines.say: Then Enron shares fell from ninety dollars and seventy-five cents to twenty-six cents in about fifteen months.

lines.text: Example: $1,000 in that one stock became $2.87. Split across 10 stocks, other 9 flat, it's $900.29.
lines.say: For example, a thousand dollars in that one stock became two dollars and eighty-seven cents. Split across ten stocks, other nine flat, it's nine hundred dollars and twenty-nine cents.

lines.text: That's diversification. It won't stop market-wide drops. It stops one rotten tree from taking every acorn.

post.title: The typical US stock lost money. Why the market didn't
post.ig:
The typical US stock lost money: a median lifetime return of -6.9% from 1926 to 2025.
Yet $1 in the whole US market grew to $15,401 over the same century.
Just 46 companies created half of the $91 trillion in stock market wealth.
At the end of 2000, 62% of Enron's 401(k) plan was Enron stock. Shares fell from $90.75 to 26 cents by Nov 2001.
Sources: Bessembinder, One Hundred Years in the U.S. Stock Markets (2026); CNBC; Congressional Research Service.
News and education, not financial advice.
